title: The Currycomb

summaryTr: Bir çiftlikte büyüyen iki kardeşten büyüğü, annesinin İstanbul'dan gönderdiği parlak kaşağıyı öfkeyle ezer ve suçu küçük kardeşinin üstüne atar. Ömer Seyfettin'in 1913 tarihli ünlü hikâyesinin sade bir İngilizce uyarlaması.
paragraphs: ## The Stable Yard

Our house stood behind the tall chestnut trees of the inner fence, and from far away it almost seemed to be hiding. Below the stable yard, under a row of silver willows, ran a small stream. We could not see it from where we played, but we could always hear it. Its quiet, sad voice belonged to every summer morning of my childhood.

That summer my mother went to Istanbul. My brother Hasan, who was one year younger than I was, stayed on the farm with me and our father, and we hardly ever left the side of old Dadaruh. He was my father's groom, the man who looked after the horses. He was slow and gentle, and he knew every animal in the stable as well as you know the faces of your own family.

Every morning, as soon as we woke up, we ran to the stable. The yard smelled of hay and warm horses and wet stone. Inside, the horses breathed and moved in the half dark, and their hooves knocked softly on the wooden floor. Dadaruh went from stall to stall and spoke to each horse in a low voice, as if it were a person. Every horse seemed to listen.

The horses were what we loved most in the world. To lead them down to the water with Dadaruh, and to ride them without a saddle, was a pleasure we never got tired of. Hasan was afraid of horses and could not ride alone. So Dadaruh always put him in front of himself and held him with one strong arm.

Hasan's favourites were the foals, the young horses with thin legs and shy eyes. He could stand for a long time at the gate of the little field, holding out a handful of barley on his open hand, the way Dadaruh had taught him. He never moved until a foal came to eat from it.
We liked the work, too. We poured barley into the feed bags, we filled the mangers with hay, and we carried the dung out of the stalls. It did not feel like work to us. It was better than any game.

At noon the yard became hot and quiet. The horses stood in the shade and drove away the flies with their tails, and the three of us sat on the cool stones by the door. Dadaruh knew a thousand things to tell us. He told us how old each horse was, which ones were fast and which ones were stubborn. Hasan's eyes grew bigger and bigger. We saw our father much less often than we saw Dadaruh. He was busy with the farm from early morning, and he came to the stable only for a moment each day.
But the best thing of all was grooming.

Dadaruh took the currycomb in his hand. A currycomb is a metal comb with small, hard teeth, and a groom uses it to clean a horse's coat. When he began, it made a quick, even sound, tik... tik... tik... tik, as regular as a clock. When I heard that sound, I could not stand still. I watched his hands. They were big and brown and cracked like old leather, but they moved so lightly that the comb seemed to dance.
"I want to do it, too!" I used to say.
Then Dadaruh would lift me onto the back of Tosun, a big, calm horse who stood like a wall, and put the currycomb in my hand.
"Go on, then," he would say. "Do it."

I rubbed the iron teeth over the horse's coat, but I could never make that lovely sound. Mine was only a rough, scraping noise. Even at night, in bed, I practised the sound with my fingers on the blanket, tik, tik, tik, and in the dark I heard Hasan laughing at me.
"Is he swinging his tail?" I asked once, because the tail was behind me and I could not see it.
"He is," said Dadaruh.
"Where? Let me look!"
I leaned over and stretched as far as I could. But from the horse's back the tail stayed out of sight.
Every morning, the moment I reached the stable, I said, "Dadaruh, today I am going to groom the horses myself."
"You can't."
"Why not?"
"Because you are too small."
"I'll do it anyway."
"Grow up first."
"When?"
"When you are as tall as a horse."
I said nothing. I looked at Tosun's huge sides and thought that I would never grow so tall.

Of all the work in the stable, grooming was the only thing I could not do. My head did not even reach the horse's belly. And it was the most wonderful job of all! Tosun seemed to love the steady tik-tik of the comb. He laid his ears back and swung his tail from side to side like a big brush. Only near the end did he become restless. Then Dadaruh would say, "Hoyt!", slap him on the rump, and start on the next horse.
## The Silver Currycomb

One day I was left alone in the stable. Hasan and Dadaruh had gone down to the stream. Suddenly a great wish to groom a horse woke up inside me, so strong that I could think of nothing else. I was tired of watching. I was tired of being small. I wanted to hear that sound come from my own hand.

I looked for the currycomb, but I could not find it. At the corner of the stable there was Dadaruh's little room. It had no window, and it was as dark as a cupboard. I went in. It smelled of leather and old hay and of Dadaruh himself. I searched the shelves. I looked among the saddles. Nothing, nothing! Then I saw a green wooden chest under the bed. I pulled it out and opened the lid. I almost shouted with joy.

Inside, shining brightly, lay a currycomb. It was one of the presents my mother had sent from Istanbul a week before. A big parcel had come that week, with something for everybody on the farm. Its metal was as bright as silver, and it was so beautiful that I held my breath when I touched it.
I snatched it up and ran to Tosun. I tried to rub it over his belly, but he would not stand still.
"Perhaps it hurts him," I said to myself.

I looked at the teeth of the beautiful comb. They were very sharp and pointed. To make them blunter, I began to rub them against the stones of the wall. When they were spoiled, I tried again. Still not one of the horses would stay quiet. Now I was angry. I wanted to take my anger out on the comb.

There was a fountain ten steps away. I ran there and laid the comb on the stone edge of the horses' trough. Then I looked for the heaviest stone I could lift from the ground. I raised it and brought it down on the comb again and again, as fast as I could. Each blow rang on the stone, and little bright pieces jumped away across the ground. I crushed it. I broke it into pieces. Then I threw the pieces into the trough.

My arms were tired, and my hands were red. I told nobody what I had done. That evening we ate our supper and went to bed, as on any other day. Before he fell asleep, Hasan whispered that one of the foals had let him touch its nose.
My father was a very strict man. One look from him was enough to make us shake with fear. Every morning, before he went out, he stopped at the stable for a moment and looked around.

That morning I was alone in the stable again. Hasan had stayed in the house with our maid, Pervin. I heard my father's steps on the stones of the yard. He walked over to the fountain and looked into the trough. At the bottom he saw the broken currycomb. He shouted to Dadaruh:
"Come here!"
My breath almost stopped. I was terribly afraid, and I do not know why. Nobody had said a word to me.
Dadaruh came running. My father took the broken pieces out of the water and put them in his hands. Dadaruh looked at them, astonished. My father asked him who had done it.
"I don't know," said Dadaruh.
My father's eyes turned to me. Before he could ask me anything, the name was out of my mouth.
"Hasan."
"Hasan?"
"Yes. Yesterday, while Dadaruh was asleep, he went into the room. He took it out of the chest. Then he crushed it on the stone of the trough."
"Why didn't you tell Dadaruh?"
"He was asleep."
"Go and call him. Let me see him."

I went out through the gate in the fence and ran along the shady road toward the house. I called Hasan. The poor boy knew nothing. He came running after me, still smiling, and he held on to my sleeve as we ran, the way small brothers do. I remember that road very well. The sun came through the leaves in small bright spots, and my heart was beating hard.
When we came back, my father was standing by the trough. Dadaruh was beside him with the broken currycomb in his hand. The pieces shone in the morning light.
"If you tell me a lie," my father said to Hasan, "I will beat you!"
"I won't lie."
"Good. Then why did you break this currycomb?"
Hasan looked at the thing in Dadaruh's hand. He did not understand. Then he shook his yellow head.
"I didn't break it," he said.
"Don't lie to me, I tell you."
"I didn't break it."
"Tell me the truth and I won't be angry," said my father. "Lying is a very bad thing."

Hasan would not change his answer. He kept saying the same words, and his voice shook. My father lost his temper. He stepped forward and hit him across the face with his open hand. The sound was very loud in the quiet yard. Tosun threw up his head.
"Shameless liar!" my father shouted. Then he turned to Dadaruh. "Take him home. Never let him come here again. Let him sit with Pervin all day long!"
Dadaruh did not look at my father, and he did not look at me. He lifted my crying brother into his arms and walked slowly toward the gate in the fence.
## The Closed Gate

After that day I always played in the stable alone. Hasan was a prisoner in the house. In the afternoons I sometimes saw him from the garden, sitting at a window beside Pervin, with his yellow head against the glass, looking toward the stable. Dadaruh went on with his work as before, but he spoke less. I still heard the stream under the willows and the tik-tik of the comb, but there was nobody beside me to share them. Hasan ate with Pervin in the kitchen now, and when my father passed the kitchen door he did not look in.

When my mother came back from Istanbul, Hasan was still not forgiven. Whenever my father had the chance, he said, "That liar." Hasan began to cry each time he remembered the slap, and it was hard to calm him down. Sometimes in the middle of a game he stopped and put his hand on his cheek, and his eyes filled with tears. My mother tried more than once to speak for him, but my father would not listen. "A boy who lies must learn," he said. My poor mother never thought for a moment that I could tell such a lie about my own brother. "Could that stupid Dadaruh have let the horses tread on it?" she used to say.

The autumn rains came, and then the snow. In the cold mornings the breath of the horses hung in white clouds under the roof of the stable, and Dadaruh warmed his hands against their necks. The stable was warm and full of the smell of hay, and Hasan stayed in the house. Then the spring came back, and the summer, and my mother went to Istanbul again. Once more we were left alone. The stable was still forbidden to Hasan. At night, in bed, he asked me what the horses were doing and whether the foals had grown. I told him what I could, and he listened without a word. I said nothing about the currycomb, and with every day it became harder to speak.

Then one day he suddenly became ill. First he said that his throat hurt. By noon he could hardly swallow, and his face was burning. A man rode off to the town as fast as his horse could go, and in the evening the doctor came. Lamps burned in every window of the house that night. The doctor looked into Hasan's throat for a long time and said a word I did not know. "Diphtheria," he said. He gave my brother some medicine, but he did not smile.

The village women from the farm filled the house. They brought birds, killed them, and wrapped them round my brother's neck. The women whispered prayers by the bed. My father never left it. He sat there without moving, with his big hands on his knees, and his face was the colour of ash. Dadaruh stood at the door with his cap in his hands, very quiet. Pervin was crying loudly.
## The Longest Night
I was not allowed in the sickroom. I stood in the passage, and at last I went up to Pervin.
"Why are you crying?" I asked her.
"Your brother is ill."
"He will get better."
"He won't."
"What will happen, then?"
"Your brother is going to die!" she said.
"Die?"

I did not understand the word. I knew that old people died, and sometimes horses. But Hasan was only one year younger than I was. I burst into tears, too. Since Hasan had fallen ill, I had been sleeping in Pervin's room. That night I could not sleep at all. The house was full of small sounds, a door, a whisper, my father's heavy steps in the passage, and under the sickroom door there was a thin line of lamplight. Each time I closed my eyes, Hasan's face came in front of me. He was crying, with the red mark of my father's hand on his cheek, and he was saying, "You lied about me! You lied about me!"
I woke Pervin.
"I want to go to Hasan," I said.
"Why?"
"I want to tell my father something."
"What do you want to tell him?"
"That I broke the currycomb. I want to say that."
"Which currycomb?"
"The one last year. You know, when my father was angry with Hasan..."

I could not finish. I was drowning in deep sobs. Crying and crying, I told Pervin everything. If I told my father now, I thought, then Hasan would hear it, and perhaps he would forgive me. Pervin was silent for a moment. Then she put her arm round me.
"Tell him tomorrow," said Pervin.
"No. I'm going now."
"Your father is sleeping now. Tell him in the morning. Hasan is asleep, too. You will kiss him, you will cry, and he will forgive you."
"All right."
"Now go to sleep."
I said nothing.

Until the morning I could not close my eyes again. I lay and listened to the clock in the hall, and the night seemed to have no end. I said the words to myself again and again, so that I would not forget them: "I broke it. It was me. I broke it." At last a cock crowed far away, the window began to turn grey, and I woke Pervin and jumped out of bed. I was in a hurry to throw out the poison inside me, the pain of my conscience. But, sadly, my poor innocent brother had died that night. The hall was cool and grey in the first light, and the door of the sickroom was closed. There we saw the imam, who led the prayers on our farm, and Dadaruh. Both of them were crying. They were waiting for my father to come out.

quiz.q: Why did Dadaruh say the narrator could not groom the horses?
options: He was afraid a horse would hurt the boy
The boy's father had forbidden it
The boy was still too small
The boy did not like horses
quiz.explainTr: Dadaruh çocuğa daha küçük olduğunu söyler; boyu at kadar olunca tımar yapabilecektir.

quiz.q: Where did the narrator find the shining currycomb?
options: In a green chest under Dadaruh's bed
Beside the fountain
On a shelf in the stable
In his mother's bag
quiz.explainTr: Kaşağıyı Dadaruh'un penceresiz odasında, yatağın altındaki yeşil tahta sandıkta bulur.

quiz.q: What did the narrator tell his father about the broken currycomb?
options: That Dadaruh had left it in the trough
That the horses had broken it
That a stranger had broken it
That Hasan had broken it while Dadaruh was asleep
quiz.explainTr: Çocuk suçu kardeşi Hasan'a atar ve Hasan'ın Dadaruh uyurken kaşağıyı kırdığını söyler.

quiz.q: What did the narrator decide to do on the night when Hasan was dying?
options: Ask the doctor for more medicine
Tell his father that he had broken the currycomb
Run to the stable to see Tosun
Give Hasan a present
quiz.explainTr: Hasan'ın ölecek olduğunu öğrenen çocuk, babasına kaşağıyı kendisinin kırdığını söylemeye karar verir.

quiz.q: Whom did the narrator see in the hall at dawn?
options: His mother, who had just come home
The doctor, who brought good news
The imam and Dadaruh, who were crying
Hasan, who felt much better
quiz.explainTr: Sabaha karşı sofada çiftlik imamını ve Dadaruh'u ağlarken görürler; Hasan o gece ölmüştür.
